Triple parabolic cosets have unique Bruhat minima

Mikey Becht    Darij Grinberg
October 22, 2026
Abstract

Abstract. A folklore result says that any parabolic double coset WI​w​WJW_{I}wW_{J} in a Coxeter group WW is an interval of the Bruhat order, provided that WIW_{I} and are finite. We include a self-contained proof, without assuming that is finite. Furthermore, we prove that each “triple coset” has a Bruhat minimum and – if are finite – a Bruhat maximum, but (in general) is not a Bruhat interval. This proves and extends a conjecture on MathOverflow #472072.

This set is called a Bruhat interval.

If is a subset of , then an element will be called a Bruhat minimum of if all satisfy . Not every subset of has a Bruhat minimum. However, when the Bruhat minimum of a subset does exist, then it is unique (since two Bruhat minima and of would have to satisfy and and therefore ) and is the unique element of having minimum length (because if is a Bruhat minimum of , then every in satisfies and therefore by Proposition 1.2 (b)).

Any Bruhat interval has the Bruhat minimum and the Bruhat maximum . However, not every subset of that has a Bruhat minimum and a Bruhat maximum is a Bruhat interval.

2 The theorems

If is any subset of , then we let denote the subgroup of generated by . It is well-known (see [BjoBre05, Proposition 2.4.1 (i) and (ii)] or [Luszti14, §9.4 and §9.6]) that is itself a Coxeter group (with simple reflections ) whose length function is a restriction of that of . It is called a parabolic subgroup of (although some authors, such as Humphreys in [Humphr90], use this word more widely for conjugates of such subgroups).

Given two subsets and of , the double cosets in are called parabolic double cosets; they have been studied by various authors from the viewpoints of descent algebras ([Solomo76]), Hecke algebras ([Curtis85]), row-semistandard tableaux ([Wildon14]) and contingency tables ([HohSka05]). Recently, the total number of distinct parabolic double cosets in a finite Coxeter group was computed ([BKPST18]).

A classical result (essentially a consequence of [Bourba02, Exercise IV.§1.3]) says that each parabolic double coset , where and are two subsets of (and where and are the corresponding parabolic subgroups of ), has a Bruhat minimum, called the “distinguished representative” of this double coset. If and are finite, then each parabolic double coset also has a Bruhat maximum, and is an interval in the Bruhat order. This appears to be a folklore result (see, e.g., [BKPST18, Proposition 2.7 (c)] and [Kobaya11]), but proofs are not easy to find in the literature, so we will include a proof for the sake of completeness:

Theorem 2.1.

Let and be two subsets of such that the parabolic subgroups and are finite. Let . Then, the double coset is a Bruhat interval.

In 2024, the MathOverflow user “fool rabbit” conjectured11 1 in https://mathoverflow.net/questions/472072/ that “parabolic triple cosets” – that is, subsets of the form for three subsets of – also have Bruhat minima and maxima when is finite. Our main goal in this note is to prove this conjecture, and even dispense with the finiteness condition to the extent possible22 2 We cannot hope to avoid requiring finiteness of in Theorem 2.3, since an infinite subset of cannot have a Bruhat maximum (after all, for any , there are only finitely many elements satisfying ).:

Theorem 2.2.

Let be three subsets of . Consider the parabolic subgroups . Let be arbitrary. Then, the subset of has a Bruhat minimum.

Theorem 2.3.

Let be three subsets of . Assume that the parabolic subgroups are finite. Let be arbitrary. Then, the subset of has a Bruhat maximum.

However, triple cosets are not as well-behaved as double cosets. In particular, even if is finite, they are not always Bruhat intervals (unlike double cosets, for which we know this from Theorem 2.1). For example, in the symmetric group (regarded as a Coxeter group of type ), the triple coset is not a Bruhat interval.

One could also define “parabolic quadruple cosets” . However, these do not satisfy an analogue of Theorem 2.2. For instance, if is the symmetric group , then the “quadruple coset” has two distinct elements of minimum length ( and ), and so has no Bruhat minimum.
